## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/02.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">bg=White Distinguishing Growth Models from Accountability Models
Defining a Year’s Growth Judgments and Accountability Models
Descriptive/Prescriptive Growth Growth Models
References

Accountability Models
Accountability mandates—like NCLB’s universal proficiency
requirement—dominate discussions of assessment outcomes.
Despite their prominence, it is important distinguish between the
judgments made by the accountability system and the assessment
derived quantities on which the judgment is based.
Accountability systems provide/impose values that allow judgments
to be made about performance at the individual or aggregate level.
A school might report 55% of its students proficient in math. Judging
this result as (in)adequate requires separate values, usually
embedded within an accountability system.
Similarly, a student scoring 500 on the grade 5 CSAP reading test is
judged unsatisfactory by the values embedded within the performance
standards and accountability system.
With the analysis of growth, it is important to distinguish between the
description of growth provided by the model and the qualification of
that value as (in)adequate by the accountability system.
D. W. Betebenner Normative Student Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">bg=White Distinguishing Growth Models from Accountability Models
Defining a Year’s Growth Judgments and Accountability Models
Descriptive/Prescriptive Growth Growth Models
References

Growth Models

Over the last decade, growth models have been used primarily to
infer effectiveness at the teacher or school level.
The foremost example being the value-added models developed by
Dr. William Sanders and used in many districts and states
nationwide to infer teacher or school effectiveness
These models and their effectiveness claims are controversial for a
number of reasons [Braun, 2005, Rubin et al., 2004].
Value-added models provide normative “effectiveness” quantities
that are difficult to interpret.
The models provide a means for accountability systems to judge
without providing a description of growth.

D. W. Betebenner Normative Student Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">bg=White Distinguishing Growth Models from Accountability Models
Defining a Year’s Growth Judgments and Accountability Models
Descriptive/Prescriptive Growth Growth Models
References

Growth Models and Implicit Values
Value-added models implicitely judge effectiveness based upon
whether teachers or schools significantly differ from mathemtically
derived expectation (i.e., “average”).
In this context, the average for a teacher of school is judged to be
neutral, significantly above average—good, and significantly
below—average bad.
Current growth to a standard methodologies implicitely judge
individual student progress based upon whether growth is sufficient
to achieve/maintain proficient status within a number of years.
Neither value-added nor growth to a standard models supply a
useful description of effectiveness/growth beyond the judgment of
(in)adequacy.
Growth models incorporated into accountability systems should
return actionable descriptions of growth/effectiveness that allow
stakeholders to more transparently impose their own values of
(in)adequacy.
D. W. Betebenner Normative Student Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/05.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">bg=White Distinguishing Growth Models from Accountability Models Actual versus Aspirational Student Growth
Defining a Year’s Growth
Describing Actual Student Growth
Descriptive/Prescriptive Growth
Exploring the Range of Aspirational Outcomes
References

Actual versus Aspirational Student Growth

It seems simple enough: Establish what constitutes a year’s growth
in a year’s time for each student.
This simplicity belies a subtle complexity.
To adequately address the notion of a year’s growth, actual growth
must be distinguished from aspirational growth.
Describe What is a current year’s growth?
Prescribe What should a current year’s growth be?
Answering the second question establishes a threshold
distinguishing adequate from inadequate growth.
To make such a distinction requires an answer to the first question
which defines a norm: What is the range of growth currently
observed?
Aspirational growth should be possible—This is Linn’s existence
proof applied at the individual level [Linn, 2003].

D. W. Betebenner Normative Student Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/06.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">bg=White Distinguishing Growth Models from Accountability Models Actual versus Aspirational Student Growth
Defining a Year’s Growth
Describing Actual Student Growth
Descriptive/Prescriptive Growth
Exploring the Range of Aspirational Outcomes
References

Describing Actual Student Growth

Measuring student growth, even with a vertical scale, is not a simple
task.
Numerous States believe that placing their tests on a vertical scale
will simplify the task of measuring student growth.
Even with an interval (or ratio) scale, growth is not easy to interpret.
Consider, for example, height.
A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
4 inches is a well understood quantity.
However, the 4 inch increase becomes fully understandable only when
placed in context of growth of other children between ages 3 and 4.
In the following discussion student growth percentiles are introduced
that provide a normative context to interpret student growth.

D. W. Betebenner Normative Student Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/11.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">bg=White Distinguishing Growth Models from Accountability Models Actual versus Aspirational Student Growth
Defining a Year’s Growth
Describing Actual Student Growth
Descriptive/Prescriptive Growth
Exploring the Range of Aspirational Outcomes
References

Student Growth Percentiles
As the figures indicate, there is a distribution of 2006 scale scores
associated with each 2005 scale score.
The average (or median) of the conditional density could be used as
a point estimate of the expected 2006 scale score given the student’s
2005 performance.
Similarly, the middle 50% of each density gives a range of scores
where one would expect such a student’s score to reside 50% of the
time.
Using quantile regression techniques, conditional densities using
more than a single prior score can be estimated.
Given a student’s prior scale scores and the associated conditional
density, their current scale score corresponds to a percentile of that
conditional distribution.
This percentile is the student’s growth percentile.
For example, a student growth percentile of 60 indicates the student’s
latest scale score exceeded 60 percent of his/her counterparts with
equal prior scores.
D. W. Betebenner Normative Student Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/12.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">bg=White Distinguishing Growth Models from Accountability Models Actual versus Aspirational Student Growth
Defining a Year’s Growth
Describing Actual Student Growth
Descriptive/Prescriptive Growth
Exploring the Range of Aspirational Outcomes
References

Student Growth Percentiles
Student growth percentiles norm each student’s growth relative to
similarly performing students.
The growth percentiles are estimated using quantile regression
techniques (Betebenner &amp; Shang, 2007; Koenker, 2005).
The percentile scale on which the growth percentiles lie allows for
easy comparison of all students.
For example, consider a low achieving student demonstrating 90th
percentile growth and a high achieving student demonstrating 10th
percentile growth.
The low achieving student grew at a rate exceeding 90 percent of
similar students.
The high achieving student grew at a rate exceeding just 10 percent of
similar students.
In this sense, the low achiever’s growth is more extraordinary than the
high achiever’s.
However, judgment of whether the student’s growth was adequate
requires external criteria.
D. W. Betebenner Normative Student Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/13.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">bg=White Distinguishing Growth Models from Accountability Models Actual versus Aspirational Student Growth
Defining a Year’s Growth
Describing Actual Student Growth
Descriptive/Prescriptive Growth
Exploring the Range of Aspirational Outcomes
References

Performance Standards and Growth Percentiles
Performance standards are the most useful external criteria needed
to define what adequate growth is.
If proficiency within 3 years is the achievement goal, then one can
examine prior growth to estimate what growth percentile is sufficient
to reach the desired outcome.
For high achieving students, modest growth percentiles are required
to maintain their position above proficiency in reading.
For low achieving (low unsatisfactory) students in reading, sustained
80th percentile growth is required to reach the desired threshold.
The process of defining (in)adequate growth is a standard setting
procedure.
Clearly, defining a year’s growth for some students as 80th
percentile or better sets a very high standard.
And defining a year’s growth for some students as 25th percentile or
better sets a low standard.
Growth standards should be equitable, reasonable, and desirable.
D. W. Betebenner Normative Student Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/14.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">bg=White Distinguishing Growth Models from Accountability Models
Defining a Year’s Growth Combining Actual and Aspirational Growth
Descriptive/Prescriptive Growth Ethics of Accountability
References

Combining Actual and Aspirational Growth

Using student growth percentiles it is simple to reconcile actual
growth measures with aspirational growth targets.
Each student receives a growth percentile derived from present
performance conditioning upon past performance.
Growth standard setting is conducted once to determine what
growth percentiles will be considered adequate and what growth
percentiles will be considered inadequate.
For example, consider a student just completing the 5th grade
Their reading was at the partially proficient level.
However, considering their 3rd and 4th grade achievement, they grew
in the last year at the 99th percentile.
Moreover, that level of growth is deemed adequate—they made at
least a year’s growth.
The following figure depicts this student’s scenario.

D. W. Betebenner Normative Student Growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/17.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">bg=White Distinguishing Growth Models from Accountability Models
Defining a Year’s Growth Combining Actual and Aspirational Growth
Descriptive/Prescriptive Growth Ethics of Accountability
References

Ethics and Accountability

Growth percentiles easily translate to probability statements and
make transparent the possibility of achievement outcomes
conditional upon where a student begins.
Given current mandates to ammeliorate achievement gaps between
ethnic and other subgroups, descriptive analyses of growth using
growth percentiles present stark alternatives.
Uniform (and challenging) achievement goals for all subgroups
results in higher—and in some cases unrealistic—growth
standards/expectations.
Is doesn’t imply ought, but ought should imply can. How can this
moral dilemma be reconciled.
Norming results by subgroup (or covarying by some other
demographic variable) is not an attractive alternative.

D. W. Betebenner Normative Student Growth</div>
```
